nodes.label: Swiss Ephemeris (product)
nodes.author: Dieter Koch, Dr. Alois Treindl
nodes.rationale: A function package of astronomical calculations for developers of astrological software, not an end-user product. Precision at least as good as the Astronomical Almanac. Consists of C source code, a Windows DLL, compressed ephemeris data files (.se1), and sample programs. Dual-licensed: GNU AGPL or the paid Swiss Ephemeris Professional License. Serves astrologers, archeoastronomers, and astronomers.

nodes.label: JPL Ephemeris DE431
nodes.rationale: Full-precision state-of-the-art JPL (NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory) planetary ephemeris, time range ~13002 BCE to 17000 CE; source of the highest-precision planetary ephemerides and basis of the Astronomical Almanac. The Swiss Ephemeris core since version 2.0 (2014) is a compression of DE431; before that it was based on DE406.

nodes.label: JPL Ephemeris DE406
nodes.rationale: Pre-2014 basis of the Swiss Ephemeris, covering 3000 BCE to 3000 CE (200 MB). Astrodienst extended its time range to 10,800 years (5401 BCE to 5399 CE) using its own numerical integration. Superseded by DE431 in SE 2.0; SE < 2.00 cannot correctly read DE431.

nodes.label: Moshier Ephemeris
nodes.author: Steve Moshier
nodes.rationale: Semi-analytical approximation of the JPL DE404 planetary and lunar ephemerides by Steve Moshier. Deviation below 1 arcsecond for the planets and a few arcseconds for the Moon; requires no data files (all data linked into code) but runs about 10x slower. Covers 3000 BCE to 3000 CE; the Moon uses a modified Chapront-Touze/Chapront lunar theory (0.5 arcsec vs DE404).

nodes.label: Swiss Ephemeris compression mechanism
nodes.author: Dr. Peter Kammeyer (USNO, 1987); Astrodienst
nodes.rationale: Idea developed by Dr. Peter Kammeyer of the US Naval Observatory (1987). For the Moon and inner planets, the differences between JPL and the analytical theory VSOP87 mean orbits (much smaller than positions) are stored as Chebyshev polynomials over one anomalistic cycle; for outer planets, JPL positions are rotated into the planet's mean plane and stored as Chebyshev polynomials over 4000 days. This reduced JPL's 2.8 GB to ~99 MB while agreeing with JPL to 1 milliarcsecond, and explains why the Swiss Ephemeris starts at the first perihelion of the last inner planet (hence shorter range than full JPL).

nodes.label: .se1 compressed ephemeris file format
nodes.rationale: Proprietary compressed ephemeris data format, file suffix .se1; each file covers 600 years. Planetary files ~500 kB (sepl_xx.se1), lunar ~1300 kB (semo_xx.se1), main-asteroid ~200 kB (seas_xx.se1). The same format is used for comet files (s9990xx.se1), planetary moons and centers of body (sat/ subdirectory), and individual additional asteroids (e.g. se00433.se1, with short 1500-2100 CE versions as s00433s.se1). Read by swe_calc()/swe_fixstar() after swe_set_ephe_path().

nodes.label: Coordinate transformation pipeline (barycentric to apparent geocentric ecliptic)
nodes.rationale: Conversions applied to raw positions read from the ephemeris files: light-time correction, barycenter-to-geocenter, light deflection by the Sun, annual aberration of light, frame bias (ICRS to J2000), precession, nutation (true equinox of date), and equatorial-to-ecliptic transformation. The team derived direct application of all transformations to barycentric speed vectors (instead of differencing three positions, which cannot beat ~0.1 arcsec/day in double precision), achieving daily-motion precision better than 0.002 arcsec/day; a position with speed takes only ~1.66x longer than without.

nodes.label: Gravity deflection for a planet passing behind the Sun (Appendix A)
nodes.author: Astrodienst; reviewed by Dr. Myles Standish (JPL)
nodes.rationale: When a planet disappears behind the solar disk no photon reaches the observer, and the Explanatory Supplement's recommendation to set the deflection to 0 would create discontinuities in the ephemeris (bad for computing transits/durations). Instead a semi-classical Newtonian model treats the Sun as transparent to electromagnetic waves but not to photons: light from an occulted planet is deflected in a transparent Sun gravity field computed by numerical integration, then multiplied by correction factor 2 to get the relativistic result. Standish: entirely reasonable as long as a reasonable solar density model (spherically symmetric standard model) is chosen.

nodes.label: Asteroid ephemerides (2.3)
nodes.rationale: Standard distribution includes main asteroids Ceres, Pallas, Juno, Vesta plus 2060 Chiron and 5145 Pholus; over 300,000 numbered asteroids are in separate downloadable files (6000-year main files; short 1500-2100 CE files free). Computed with a modified version of Steve Moshier's numerical integrator (which can rebuild DE200), from Lowell Observatory orbital elements (one extra digit) and JPL DASTCOM elements for close-Sun orbiters (to account for relativity). Mutual perturbations of Ceres/Pallas/Vesta included by iterative integration; accuracy is limited by input-element uncertainty, not the algorithm. Orbits that become chaotic (e.g. 1862 Apollo before 1870 CE) terminate the ephemeris generation to avoid meaningless data.

nodes.label: Chiron (2060) and Pholus (5145)
nodes.rationale: Centaur objects. Chiron can be well computed only between 700 CE and 4650 CE because close encounters with Saturn make its orbital elements chaotic outside that range (earlier Chiron ephemerides for Jesus/Cesar's birth charts are meaningless). Pholus, discovered 1992, has orbital characteristics similar to Chiron's; its ephemeris is reliable from 1500 CE and will probably be corrected by several arc minutes during the 20th century.

nodes.label: 99942 Apophis
nodes.rationale: Near-Earth asteroid (700 km diameter, apparent 2.5 arcmin) that will have a very close encounter with Earth around 13 April 2029; the Swiss Ephemeris entry was created from JPL Horizons data and is particularly uncertain after that date. To be updated after the 2029 encounter for accuracy at least until 2036.

nodes.label: Planetary Centers of Body (COB) and Planetary Moons (2.4)
nodes.author: Walter Pullen, Dieter Koch
nodes.rationale: All earlier ephemerides and astrology software provided only the barycenter of a planet system (e.g. Jupiter plus its moons), not the planet's body center; the max geocentric angular difference is small (e.g. 0.075 arcsec for Jupiter). Since SE 2.10, centers of body (computed as planetary moon number 99, e.g. 9599 for Jupiter) and planetary moons (numbering 9401-999x, files in the sat/ subdirectory) are available, downloaded from JPL Horizons and compressed with the chopt software; performance is not as good as for barycenters and the time range is currently limited to 1900-2047.

nodes.label: Comet and interstellar object ephemerides (2.5)
nodes.rationale: Ephemerides of a few selected comets under pseudo-MPC numbers 999032-999047 plus 1I/'Oumuamua: 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko, C/2020 F3 (Neowise), 1P/Halley, Hale-Bopp, Comet West, 'Oumuamua. Downloaded from JPL Horizons and compressed in the Swiss Ephemeris .se1 data file format.

nodes.label: Fixed star database (2.6)
nodes.author: Steve Moshier (base); Valentin Abramov; SIMBAD
nodes.rationale: Database of about 800 fixed stars computable with the swe_fixstar() function, precision about 0.001 arcsec. Originally based on the star catalogue of Steve Moshier; improved in 1999 by Valentin Abramov (reordered by constellation, added stars/names/spellings). Updated from the SIMBAD database in Feb 2006 (v1.70), and in Jan 2011 (v1.77) a new file sefstars.txt with a SIMBAD-compatible format was created and continues to be updated.

nodes.label: Hypothetical (fictitious) astrological bodies (2.7)
nodes.rationale: Astrological factors with no astronomical/physical basis, included for service to astrologers. Includes: Uranian/Hamburg planets (Cupido, Hades, Zeus, Kronos, Apollon, Admetos, Vulkanus, Poseidon - from Witte & Siegrun, refined by James Neely; circular orbits, zero inclination, physically unrealistic), Transpluto (Isis, postulated by M.E. Sevin 1946), Harrington (Planet X 1988), Nibiru (Zacharia Sitchin, retrograde), Vulcan (intra-Mercurian, L.H. Weston), Selena/White Moon (Russian 'second Moon'), Dr. Waldemath's Black Moon, and the Planet Xs of Leverrier, Adams, Lowell and Pickering (precursors of Neptune/Pluto). SWISSEPH uses James Neely's revised elements for the Uranian planets. Can be computed with any of the three ephemeris flags.

nodes.label: Uranian (Hamburg) planets: Cupido, Hades, Zeus, Kronos, Apollon, Admetos, Vulkanus, Poseidon
nodes.author: Witte & Siegrun (inventors); James Neely (refined elements)
nodes.rationale: Hypothetical transneptunian 'planets' invented by German astrologers Witte and Siegrun; orbits are highly unrealistic (some perfect circles, zero inclination, eccentricities smaller than Venus'). Swisseph uses James Neely's revised orbital elements (Matrix Journal VII, 1980) because they agree better with the original position tables of Witte and Siegrun. None identified with any real transneptunian object discovered since 1992.

nodes.label: Transpluto (Isis)
nodes.author: M.E. Sevin (1946)
nodes.rationale: Hypothetical planet postulated in 1946 by French astronomer M.E. Sevin to explain unexplained gravitational perturbations of Uranus and Neptune; since superseded by better data (residuals too small to postulate a new planet). SWISSEPH elements taken from 'Die Sterne' 3/1952 p.70; no orbital inclination given, so computed positions show a small ecliptic latitude. Can only provide a rough position (arc-minute accuracy illusory).

nodes.label: Harrington and Nibiru (speculative Planet X)
nodes.author: Harrington (1988); Christian Woeltje (Nibiru elements, after Sitchin)
nodes.rationale: Harrington: Planet X attempt from Uranus/Neptune perturbations, Astronomical Journal 96(4) Oct 1988, precision only +/-30 degrees. Nibiru: speculative planet from Zecharia Sitchin's 'paleoastronomy'; elements supplied by Christian Woeltje - bizarre orbit, clockwise (retrograde) direction, 3600 year period, extremely eccentric (perihelion in the asteroid belt, aphelion ~12x Pluto's distance).

nodes.label: Planet X of Leverrier, Adams, Lowell, Pickering
nodes.rationale: The hypothetical planets that led to the discovery of Neptune (Leverrier, Adams, good around 1840) and Pluto (Lowell, Pickering). Their enormous deviations from true Neptune/Pluto (2 degrees between 1830 and 1850, growing fast beyond) may interest astrologers. Computed via swetest with -fFPLBLR (heliocentric) and the -p8 (Neptune) flag.

nodes.label: Sidereal ephemerides and the ayanamsha (2.8)
nodes.rationale: Sidereal astrology uses a zodiac fixed to the stars rather than the vernal point (tropical). The precession of the equinoxes (~1 arcminute per 71.6 years) makes the two drift apart (over 20 degrees today). Sidereal positions are computed as sidereal_position = tropical_position - ayanamsha(t), where the ayanamsha is the distance of the vernal point from the sidereal Aries point. The Swiss Ephemeris implements more than forty ayanamshas (numbered 0-46), from the Babylonian tradition (Fagan/Bradley, Kugler, Huber, Britton), the Hipparchan tradition (Mercier), the Indian tradition (Suryasiddhanta/K0s, Aryabhata/K0a, Lahiri, Krishnamurti), and galactic-center/galactic-equator-based ones (Mardysk, Gil Brand, Cochrane, Fiorenza).

nodes.label: Fagan/Bradley ayanamsha (No. 0)
nodes.author: Donald Bradley; Cyril Fagan
nodes.rationale: The standard western sidereal ayanamsha: ayanamsha 24 degrees 02' 31.36" for 1 Jan 1950, placing Spica at 29 degrees 06'05" Virgo (without aberration), per Fagan and Bradley. Cyril Fagan reintroduced the old Babylonian zodiac (Spica near 29 degrees 00' Virgo) into western astrology around 1950; Peter Huber and J.P. Britton offered refinements of the Babylonian zero point.

nodes.label: Lahiri ayanamsha (No. 1, Indian standard)
nodes.author: N. C. Lahiri / Indian Calendar Reform Committee (1955)
nodes.rationale: The Indian standard ayanamsha, introduced by the Indian Calendar Reform Committee in 1955: 23 degrees 15' 00" (later corrected to 23 degrees 15' 00".658) on 21 March 1956, Spica (Chitra) at 179 degrees 58'59". Named after N. C. Lahiri, a member of the committee; it is the basis of the ayanamsha values in the Indian Astronomical Ephemeris, IENA, and Rastriya Panchang. Note: the 'mean ayanamsha' value given by IAE is really a true ayanamsha (includes nutation, relative to the true equinox of date).

nodes.label: Krishnamurti ayanamshas (Nos. 5, 45)
nodes.author: K.S. Krishnamurti (1908-1972)
nodes.rationale: Two ayanamshas named after the Indian astrologer K.S. Krishnamurti, very close to Lahiri (difference of only 4-5 arcminutes). No. 45 (Krishnamurti/Senthilathiaban) assumes zero ayanamsha on 21 March 291 CE, 6:10:29 TT, derived using the Swiss Ephemeris with precession Vondrak 2011. No. 5 is derived from his ayanamsha table (22.363889 for 1 Jan 1900), taken over via Graham Dawson's Solar Fire and Robert Hand's Nova.

nodes.label: Galactic Center / Galactic Equator ayanamshas
nodes.rationale: Ayanamshas based on the galactic center or the galactic node (intersection of the galactic equator with the ecliptic) rather than a fixed star, because fixed stars have proper motion and no truly 'fixed' reference. Includes: Galactic Center at 0 Sagittarius (No. 17, added 1999 per D. Koch), 0 Capricorn (Cochrane, No. 40), the Ehrnst Wilhelm Dhrvu middle-of-Mula (No. 36), Rafael Gil Brand golden section (No. 30), Mardysk/Skydram (No. 34, 1991), Fiorenza (No. 41), and the Ardra (No. 33) variant. Bruno Huber noted that every time the vernal point enters a new tropical sign the galactic center enters the next.

nodes.label: On which ecliptic the ayanamsha is measured (2.8.12)
nodes.rationale: The traditional method (ayanamsha measured on the ecliptic of the start epoch, subtracted from positions referred to the ecliptic of date) is not fully correct because the ecliptic plane itself moves (planetary precession changes the obliquity by about 47"/century and the vernal point wobbles). SE >= 2.09 offers consistent alternatives: (2) ayanamsha computed relative to the ecliptic of the end epoch, and (3) projection of the planetary positions onto the ecliptic of t0, which also enables standard equinoxes (J2000, J1900, B1950) and precession-corrected transits. A fixed-star-bound ecliptic is implemented for selected anchor stars (Spica at 180 degrees, Revati at 359 degrees 50', Pushya at 106 degrees, Mula at 240 degrees, Galactic Center).

nodes.label: Precession model Vondrak/Capitaine/Wallace 2011
nodes.author: Vondrak, Capitaine, Wallace (A&A 534, A22, 2011)
nodes.rationale: The precession model used by the Swiss Ephemeris from version 1.78 on, valid for about +/- 200 millennia (versus P03/Capitaine 2003 previously, and Laskar 1986 outside that range). It enables fixed-star position calculations back to 15000-33000 BCE for prehistoric cave-painting research, while Sun/Moon/planets remain restricted to the ephemeris time range. The IAU currently recommends IAU 2006 (Capitaine); the Swiss Ephemeris uses Vondrak 2011 which is particularly good for remote epochs. Using a different precession model for the ayanamsha than for the underlying tropical ephemerides is an inconsistent approach (2.8.11), though the ayanamsha is adjusted automatically so sidereal positions stay stable.

nodes.label: Heliacal events of Moon, planets and stars (5.1)
nodes.author: Reijs (2003), Koch (2009); criterion of Schaefer (1993, 2000)
nodes.rationale: Heliacal rising/setting (evening first, morning last) calculations included since SE 1.76, important for ancient Babylonian/Greek astronomy and for the Islamic, Babylonian and ancient Jewish calendars. Based on Schaefer's visibility criterion as implemented by Reijs and Koch, depending on: position and magnitude of the object, the observer's location and optical properties (age, acuity, instruments), meteorological circumstances (astronomical extinction coefficient from pressure/temperature/humidity), and the contrast between object and sky background. Functions swe_heliacal_ut() and swe_vis_limit_mag(); limited to latitudes between 60S and 60N because heliacal phenomena become erratic beyond.

nodes.label: Eclipses, occultations, risings, settings, planetary phenomena (5.2)
nodes.rationale: Functions to search for solar/lunar eclipses and lunar occultations globally or at a given geographic position, to compute the circumstances of an eclipse (how), and to find where an eclipse is central; plus risings and settings, midheaven and lower-heaven transits, height above the horizon (refracted and true), phase angle, illuminated fraction, elongation, apparent diameter and apparent magnitude - all also for stars. Corresponding API: swe_sol_eclipse_when_loc/glob, swe_sol_eclipse_how/where, swe_lun_eclipse_when_loc/glob, swe_lun_occult_when_loc/glob, swe_rise_trans, swe_pheno, swe_azalt.

nodes.label: Astrological house systems (6.2)
nodes.rationale: House cusp methods implemented: Placidus (Placidus de Titus 1590-1668, division of the semidiurnal/seminocturnal arcs, 11th cusp at 2/3), Koch/GOH (invented by Zanninger and Specht, made known by Walter Koch), Regiomontanus (Johannes Muller), Campanus, equal systems, Porphyry/Sripati, Pullen SD (Sinusoidal Delta, 1994) and Pullen SR (Sinusoidal Ratio, 2016), axial rotation systems (Meridian, Carter poli-equatorial), Morinus, horizontal, Polich-Page, Alcabitus, Gauquelin sectors (36 sectors with plus/minus zones), Krusinski/Pisa/Goelzer, APC, and Sunshine (Bob Makransky). Beyond the polar circle Placidus/Koch cusps may not exist; the function then switches to Porphyry houses and returns a warning, keeping the Ascendant in the eastern hemisphere.

nodes.label: Improvement of the Placidus house calculation in SE 2.09
nodes.author: D. Senthilathiaban (reported the issue)
nodes.rationale: Before SE 2.09 the Placidus cusps were calculated with only two iterations, giving 1-arcsecond accuracy only up to about latitude 56 degrees. Fixed in SE 2.09 by a variable number of iterations that stops on convergence, with n=100 as the maximum; if it does not converge the calculation switches to Porphyry cusps and returns a warning.

nodes.label: Delta T (TT - UT) (Ch. 7)
nodes.rationale: Delta T is the difference between Terrestrial Time (TT, formerly Ephemeris Time; uniform atomic-clock time) and Universal Time (UT, based on Earth rotation). Earth's rotation decreases at roughly 0.5-1 sec/year, irregularly and unpredictably; past values are only determinable from observations (solar/lunar eclipses since about 720 BCE, star occultations since about 1700, IERS since 1962). SE >= 2.06 uses Stephenson/Morrison/Hohenkerk (2016) for epochs before 1948, AA K8-9 from 1955, and USNO/IERS values from 1974; Delta T = TAI-UT1 + 32.184 sec. The tidal acceleration ndot differs by ephemeris (DE431: -25.80, LE405/406: -25.826, ELP2000/DE200: -23.8946 arcsec/century^2). swe_calc_ut() absorbs this conversion so users can work in Universal Time.

nodes.label: Comparison with JPL Horizons (53 mas offset; Appendix C)
nodes.rationale: From v1.70 the Swiss Ephemeris reproduces the astrometric JPL Horizons positions precisely, but the apparent positions show a constant ~53 mas RA offset because Horizons uses IERS Conventions 1996 (precession IAU 1976 Lieske, nutation IAU 1980 Wahr) while the Swiss Ephemeris and the Astronomical Almanac use IERS Conventions 2003/2010. SE >= 2.00 reproduces Horizons to about 1 mas using the IERS Earth orientation parameter files (eop_1962_today.txt, eop_finals.txt); SE >= 2.07 does so over the whole Horizons time range. Appendix C gives ten concrete comparison tests (ICRF/J2000, inertial apparent, equinox-of-date, heliocentric, pre-1962, barycenter vs planet, COB, geocentric/planetocentric moons, topocentric).

nodes.label: Astronomical Almanac agreement
nodes.rationale: The Swiss Ephemeris reproduces Astronomical Almanac sample positions to the last digit (better than 0.001 arcsecond): AA 1984/1995/1996/1997 (DE200-based) and AA2006, AA2011, AA2013 (with the IAU resolutions). SE uses JPL DE431 since 2014 and the Almanac uses DE430 since 2016; the two still perfectly agree. The Explanatory Supplement to the Astronomical Almanac provides the algorithms and constants used for the conversions from the JPL barycentric equatorial Cartesian coordinates to apparent geocentric ecliptic positions.

nodes.label: Swiss Ephemeris dual licensing model
nodes.author: Astrodienst AG
nodes.rationale: The Swiss Ephemeris is a programmer's toolset (not an end-user product) released under a dual license: (a) GNU Affero GPL (AGPL) - the developer's whole project must be AGPL or compatible; or (b) the Swiss Ephemeris Professional License (paid, one-time fixed fee per commercial project: CHF 750 first, CHF 400 each additional, CHF 1550 unlimited). The choice must be made before distributing software containing parts of Swiss Ephemeris or activating any public service. All software and data are in the public download area; the Professional license is a legal document only.

nodes.label: Mean Lunar Node and Mean Lunar Apogee (Lilith, Black Moon)
nodes.rationale: The mean node and mean apogee are the (mean) orbital elements of the mean Keplerian lunar orbit, taken from planetary theory VSOP87; in astrology the mean apogee is the 'Black Moon' (mean Lilith). There is no apparent position for these mathematical points. The Swiss Ephemeris apogee differs from Joelle de Gravelaine's 'Lilith, der schwarze Mond' (Astrodata 1990) by several arc minutes because the mean apogee/perigee moves along the mean lunar orbit (inclination ~5 degrees) and must be projected onto the ecliptic; de Gravelaine did not do this projection. Using the barycenter instead of the geocenter as the first focus would cause a monthly oscillation of ~+/-40 arc minutes (neglected).

nodes.label: True Lunar Node (2.2.2)
nodes.rationale: The true node is the osculating node of the momentary (osculating-ellipse) lunar orbit: the intersection line of the momentary orbital plane of the Moon and the plane of the ecliptic, and it is connected with eclipses. When the Moon is in exact conjunction with the true node it has exactly zero ecliptic latitude (unlike the mean node). The 'true' node is only truly true twice a month (at the node passages); in between it is approximated from the osculating ellipse. Computed from all three ephemerides; for at least one-arcsecond precision use JPL or the Swiss Ephemeris (max difference ~0.1 arcsec; Moshier differs by ~70 arcsec).

nodes.label: Osculating Apogee / True Lilith / True Dark Moon (2.2.3)
nodes.rationale: The position of 'true Lilith' is the osculating apogee of the momentary lunar orbit; it is 'true' only twice a month (conjunction and opposition with the Moon). Unlike the node it contains the concept of an ellipse, and the lunar orbit is far from being a two-body ellipse, so the osculating apogee oscillates ~+/-30 degrees about the mean apogee - an artifact of the two-body reduction (the actual apogee's deviation from the mean never exceeds 5 degrees). The New International Ephemerides (Santoni/Ed. St. Michel) and de Gravelaine give a slightly different 'true Lilith' (error of order 20 arcmin). Max difference JPL vs Swiss ~0.9 arcsec; JPL vs Moshier ~360 arcsec (6 arcmin). Several correction-table approaches (Santoni, Henry Gouchon, Dieter Koch's 'Meridian' 1/95) are not included.

nodes.label: Interpolated or Natural Apogee and Perigee / Lilith and Priapus (2.2.4)
nodes.author: Dieter Koch; Juan Revilla
nodes.rationale: A more sensible solution than the osculating apogee: interpolate between the real passages of the Moon through its apogees and perigees (Koch's 'interpolated'/'natural', Revilla's 'realistic' apogee and perigee, astrological Lilith and Priapus). The supporting points are too far apart for conventional interpolation, so Koch derived an interpolation method from the analytical lunar theory (in Moshier's solution form), which also keeps the curve and its derivation continuous. Implemented from Swiss Ephemeris version 1.70 on (SE_INTP_APOG=21, SE_INTP_PERG=22).

nodes.label: Planetary Nodes and Apsides (2.2.5)
nodes.rationale: Planetary nodes can be defined as the axis from the intersection of two orbital planes (e.g. Mars orbit with ecliptic), as the two points where the orbit crosses the ecliptic plane (geocentrically different from the axis definition for the outer planets), or as instantaneous intersection points; apsidal points are perihelion/aphelion or the second focal points ('black stars', used by Bernard Fitzwalter and Raymond Henry). Special cases: the Earth (uses the heliocentric motion of the Earth-Moon barycenter EMB, no node of its own) and the Sun ('Black Sun' at ~13 Capricorn perigee and 'Diamond' in Cancer, used by George Bode and Liduina Schmed). Mean nodes/apsides come from VSOP87 (not for Pluto/asteroids; NASA DE200 mean elements rejected as too short-term); osculating nodes/apsides beyond Jupiter are preferably computed from a barycentric ellipse because the heliocentric orbit of slow planets (Neptune in particular) is not even elliptical. Mean vs osculating vs interpolated differ considerably (e.g. Neptune's mean vs heliocentric osculating perihelion by more than 3 degrees).

nodes.label: Sidereal Time (6.1)
nodes.rationale: Swiss Ephemeris versions until 1.80 used the IAU 1976 formula for sidereal time. Since 2.00 it uses sidereal time based on the IAU 2006 precession/nutation model, which is only good over the JPL DE431 range (1850-2050); outside that period a solution based on the long-term Vondrak 2011 precession, IAU2000 nutation and the Simon & alii mean motion of the Earth is used, with constants added to keep the function continuous. Computed with swe_sidtime()/swe_sidtime0().

nodes.label: House cusps beyond the polar circle (6.4)
nodes.rationale: Beyond the polar circle, if Placidus/Koch cusps cannot be computed, the function automatically switches to Porphyry houses and returns a warning; the Ascendant is kept in the eastern hemisphere, and if the MC falls below the horizon (Campanus/Regiomontanus) the MC and IC are swapped so the whole system is oriented clockwise. Similar handling applies to the Vertex and horizon-house system for tropic birthplaces (Vertex always in the western hemisphere, 0 Aries/Libra on the equator). Placalc (the 1988 predecessor) gave priority to the MC; Swiss Ephemeris gives priority to the Ascendant (a model considered more natural by Treindl and Koch).

nodes.label: Ceres - application program for asteroid astrology (2.3.7)
nodes.author: Dieter Koch
nodes.rationale: An application program by Dieter Koch that computes lists for asteroid astrology: natal positions, synastries/transits, composite charts, progressions, primary directions; geocentric, heliocentric, topocentric and house horoscopes; and lists sorted by position in the zodiac, by asteroid name, or by declination. Found in the Swiss Ephemeris download area in the folder 'programs'.

nodes.label: Nutation (IAU 2006 model)
nodes.rationale: A short-period oscillation of the vernal equinox caused by the Moon's gravity on the equatorial bulge of the Earth; the period equals the lunar node cycle (~18.6 years) and the difference between the true and mean vernal point is always below 17 arcseconds. SE 2.0 uses the IAU 2006 nutation model (from 1.70 it used IAU 2000; older versions used IAU 1980/Wahr). Nutation is already added internally by swe_calc(), but SE_ECL_NUT (-1) can be computed to obtain it as a separate value.

nodes.label: Swiss Ephemeris release history (v1.00 1997 to v2.10.03 2022)
nodes.rationale: Milestones: v1.00 (1997) initial release; 1.20 topocentric planets; 1.31 eclipses; 1.40 planetary phenomena; 1.50 sidereal ephemerides; 1.60 swe_calc_ut/swe_fixstar_ut (Universal Time input); 1.64 occultations and new Delta T; 1.66 Morinus houses; 1.70 IAU resolutions up to 2005 and interpolated lunar apsides; 1.74 dual AGPL/Professional licensing; 1.76 heliacal events; 1.78 Vondrak 2011 precession; 2.00 based on JPL DE431; 2.03 thread-safe; 2.09 improved Placidus houses; 2.10 planetary moons; 2.10.03 moon magnitude update. Versions before 2.00 cannot read DE431.

nodes.label: Apparent versus true planetary positions (Ch. 3)
nodes.rationale: The Swiss Ephemeris provides apparent (geocentric, corrected for light-time and aberration) or true positions. Apparent means where the planet is seen, not where it actually is (finite light travel time); with planets the effect is below 1 arc minute. Astrology mostly works with apparent positions, though it is impossible to derive astrological effects from any of the four fundamental forces, and some argue true positions are more convincing for synchronistic effects. The software supports both via the SEFLG_TRUEPOS flag, plus astrometric positions used by astronomers relative to fixed stars; apparent JPL-Horizons-style positions are reproducible with the JPL-Horizons flag bits.

nodes.label: Geocentric, topocentric, heliocentric, barycentric, planetocentric positions (Ch. 4)
nodes.rationale: Common ephemerides give the position seen from the center of the Earth (geocentric). Topocentric positions (swe_set_topo() plus topocentric flag) are referred to the observer's geographic birth place and require also the altitude above sea; the effect is about 1 arc second with the Moon and more with other bodies. Heliocentric positions are seen from the Sun, barycentric from the solar-system barycenter (not fully implemented, JPL/Swiss only, no nodes/apogees), and planetocentric (swe_calc_pctr) positions are seen from some other object. For the Sun, lunar nodes and apogees a heliocentric request returns zero with no error.

nodes.label: House position and Gauquelin sector position of a planet (6.5, 6.6)
nodes.rationale: swe_house_pos() gives the actual house position of a body (not just the sign), which can differ from the naive chart-drawing position because bodies have an ecliptic latitude; three methods (ignoring latitude, using true position, or the rise/set times) are supported, and methods 2 and 3 also work for polar/circumpolar bodies using the Otto Ludwig midnight/midday-culmination trick. The Gauquelin sector position (swe_gauquelin_sector()) divides the diurnal/nocturnal arcs into 36 sectors for statistical astrology, with plus/minus zones; beyond the polar circle Placidus positions are still provided.

nodes.label: What is missing (Ch. 30)
nodes.rationale: A short section noting capabilities not yet present in the Swiss Ephemeris (e.g. acronychal risings/settings of superior planets and stars were deferred to a future version, and comparison of alternative visibility criteria such as Schorch's 1928 and Hoffman's criteria was still planned).

nodes.label: VSOP87 analytical planetary theory
nodes.rationale: The IAU analytical (Fourier-series) planetary theory used as the reference mean orbits. The Swiss Ephemeris compression stores the difference between the JPL numerical ephemeris and the VSOP87 mean orbits (far smaller than the position itself). The mean planetary nodes and apsides (Sun, Moon, Mercury-Neptune) are also taken from VSOP87; NASA's DE200-based mean elements are not used because they are limited to a 250-year period with linear rates only.

nodes.label: swetest - Swiss Ephemeris test program
nodes.rationale: Command-line test program (swetest.c/swetest.exe) in the Swiss Ephemeris distribution that computes planetary positions with any combination of flags and is used to verify agreement with JPL Horizons, the Astronomical Almanac, and the Indian Astronomical Ephemeris. It is the reference for the Appendix C comparison tests and for computing the hypothetical Planet X bodies.
